text: Read the extract: 'Why, look you, how you storm! I would be friends with you and have your love, Forget the shames that you have stain'd me with, Supply your present wants, and take no doit Of usance for my moneys, and you'll not hear me: This is kind I offer.' Who is speaking, to whom, and what does he propose immediately after this?
modelAnswer: Shylock is speaking to Antonio in a street in Venice, in the presence of Bassanio, after Antonio has come to ask Shylock for a loan of three thousand ducats for Bassanio. Shylock complains that despite his conciliatory offer of friendship and an interest-free loan, Antonio will not even listen to him. Immediately after this speech, Shylock proposes that, as a merry sport, Antonio should sign a bond agreeing that if the money is not repaid within the stated time, Shylock may cut off a pound of flesh from Antonio's body nearest his heart.
keyPoints: Shylock addresses Antonio, offering friendship and an interest-free loan despite past insults
The scene takes place on a street in Venice, with Bassanio also present
Shylock proposes the bond of a pound of flesh as a 'merry sport' if the loan is not repaid on time

text: With reference to the casket scene, what test had Portia's father devised for her suitors, and what oath did the suitors have to take before making their choice?
modelAnswer: Portia's father, in his will, devised a lottery of three caskets — of gold, silver and lead — one of which contains Portia's portrait. Whichever suitor chooses the casket with her picture inside wins her hand in marriage. Before attempting the choice, every suitor had to swear an oath that if he chose wrongly, he would never reveal which casket he chose, never marry any woman afterwards, and would leave Belmont immediately.
keyPoints: Three caskets (gold, silver, lead) — the one with Portia's portrait decides her husband
Suitors must swear never to disclose their choice if wrong
A wrong choice also means they can never marry and must leave at once

text: 'Still more fool I shall appear by the time I linger here: With one fool's head I came to woo, But I go away with two.' Who speaks these lines, and in what state of mind? What schedule had he found in the casket he chose?
modelAnswer: These lines are spoken by the Prince of Morocco, after he has opened the golden casket — inscribed 'Who chooseth me shall gain what many men desire' — only to find a skull with a scroll inside, instead of Portia's portrait. He is bitterly disappointed and mortified, admitting to his own foolishness for being misled by outward show. The scroll (schedule) inside mocked those who judge by appearances, warning that 'all that glisters is not gold' and that his judgement, like his choice, had grown old without growing wise.
keyPoints: Morocco opened the gold casket, expecting to win Portia
He found a skull and a scroll instead of her portrait
The scroll warns against being deceived by outward, glittering appearances

text: Read the extract: 'If I live to be as old as Sibylla, I will die as chaste as Diana, unless I be obtained by the manner of my father's will.' What is Portia saying about her marriage here, and what are her true feelings towards the suitors who have come to try their luck at the caskets?
modelAnswer: Portia is saying that she will remain unmarried and chaste all her life unless a suitor wins her by correctly choosing the right casket, as laid down in her father's will. Although this means she has no control over who she may marry, she expresses relief that the present group of wearisome suitors are so 'reasonable' (sensible) that they have decided to leave without attempting the lottery at all — she says she 'dotes on their very absence' and prays for their safe, swift departure, showing she is not attracted to any of them.
keyPoints: Portia is bound by her father's will to marry only the man who chooses the right casket
She compares herself to the chaste goddess Diana if no suitor succeeds
She is relieved and amused that the current suitors are leaving without even trying, as she dislikes them all

text: Read the extract: 'Nature hath framed strange fellows in her time: Some that will evermore peep through their eyes, And laugh like parrots at a bag-piper; And other of such vinegar aspect, That they'll not show their teeth in way of smile, Though Nestor swear the jest be laughable.' Explain, in your own words, the two types of 'strange fellows' that nature has framed, as described by Salarino.
modelAnswer: Salarino describes two opposite kinds of people that nature creates. The first type are people who are always cheerful and laugh uncontrollably at anything, even something as ordinary as the sound of a bagpiper, much like a parrot laughing at everything it sees. The second type are extremely sour and grim-faced people who never smile, even if the wisest and most respected man (Nestor) swears that a joke is genuinely funny. Salarino uses this to explain why some men, like Antonio, are naturally melancholic by temperament rather than through any particular worry.
keyPoints: First type: people who laugh at everything, even trivial things, like parrots at a bagpiper
Second type: sour-faced people who never smile even at a genuinely funny joke
Salarino uses this contrast to suggest Antonio's sadness may just be his natural temperament

text: Read the extract: 'I never heard a passion so confused, so strange, outrageous, and so variable, as the dog Jew did utter in the streets: "My daughter! O my ducats! O my daughter!"' Who is referred to as the 'dog Jew'? Explain how the Jew's lamentation over his daughter and his money, in the same breath, adds to the humour of the play.
modelAnswer: The 'dog Jew' refers to Shylock, described contemptuously by Salarino. The humour arises because Shylock's lament jumbles his grief over his runaway daughter, Jessica, together with his grief over the ducats and jewels she has stolen from him, so that he seems unable to decide which loss pains him more — crying out for his daughter and his money in almost the same breath. This confusion of a father's love with a miser's greed makes Shylock appear both pitiable and ridiculous to the Venetians who mock him in the streets.
keyPoints: Shylock is mockingly called the 'dog Jew' by the Venetians
He cries about his runaway daughter Jessica and his stolen ducats almost interchangeably
The comic effect comes from his inability to separate his love for his daughter from his greed for his money

text: Read the extract: 'Launcelot: But I pray you, ergo, old man, ergo, I beseech you, talk you of young Master Launcelot? ...the young gentleman...is, indeed, deceased; or, as you would say in plain terms, gone to heaven.' Who was Gobbo, and what reasons does Launcelot (his son) give for wanting to leave his present master's service?
modelAnswer: Old Gobbo is Launcelot's blind, elderly father, who has come looking for his son Launcelot without recognising him, and asks a disguised Launcelot for news of 'young Master Launcelot'. Launcelot plays a trick on him, pretending his son is dead, before revealing his true identity. Launcelot wants to leave the service of his present master, Shylock, because Shylock starves him — he complains he is 'famished' in Shylock's service, as the Jew is a miser who provides little food. He wishes instead to serve Bassanio, who he has heard gives rare new liveries (clothes) to his servants and treats them generously.
keyPoints: Old Gobbo, Launcelot's blind father, fails to recognise his own son
Launcelot wants to leave Shylock's service because he is half-starved there
He wishes to serve the generous Bassanio instead, who is known for treating servants well

text: Read the extract: '...why thou loss upon loss! The thief gone with so much, and so much to find the thief; and no satisfaction, no revenge...' Who is the thief Shylock refers to, what had the thief stolen, and what does Tubal bring him news of?
modelAnswer: The 'thief' Shylock refers to is his own daughter, Jessica, who has eloped with the Christian Lorenzo, taking with her a large sum of Shylock's ducats and precious jewels. Shylock is in anguish because he has spent money trying to track her down, with no success and no revenge gained. Tubal, Shylock's friend and fellow Jew, has just returned from Genoa, where he could not find Jessica, but he brings Shylock the welcome news that Antonio's ships have been reported lost at sea — information that delights Shylock and fuels his plan for revenge against Antonio.
keyPoints: Jessica, Shylock's daughter, is the 'thief' who eloped with Lorenzo, taking ducats and jewels
Tubal has returned from Genoa having failed to find Jessica
Tubal's news of Antonio's lost ships delights Shylock and feeds his desire for revenge

text: Read the extract: 'To bait fish withal: if it will feed nothing else, it will feed my revenge. He hath disgraced me, and hindered me half a million; laughed at my losses, mocked at my gains, scorned my nation, thwarted my bargains, cooled my friends, heated mine enemies; and what's his reason? I am a Jew.' In this famous speech, how does Shylock use Christian conduct to justify his desire for revenge?
modelAnswer: Shylock argues that Jews are physically and emotionally no different from Christians — they have eyes, hands, senses, affections and passions just like them. He then points out that Christians themselves teach revenge by example: if a Christian is wronged by another Christian, his natural response (by Christian example) is revenge. Shylock reasons that since Christians practise revenge when wronged, he, a Jew wronged by a Christian (Antonio), is merely following the very lesson Christians themselves have taught him by their own conduct.
keyPoints: Shylock insists Jews share the same humanity, senses and feelings as Christians
He points out that Christians themselves set the example of taking revenge when wronged
He uses this Christian 'example' to justify his own planned revenge on Antonio

text: Read the extract: 'They vanish tongue-tied in their guiltiness. Go you down that way towards the Capitol; This way will I. Disrobe the images If you do find them deck'd with ceremonies.' What does Flavius mean by 'images' and 'ceremonies', and what instruction does he give his companion?
modelAnswer: Flavius is speaking to Marullus, his fellow tribune. The 'images' refer to statues of Julius Caesar that have been decorated around the city, and the 'ceremonies' refer to the festive decorations (scarves, trophies) that over-enthusiastic commoners have hung on them to celebrate Caesar's triumph. Flavius instructs Marullus to go towards the Capitol while he takes another route, and both are to strip away ('disrobe') any such decorations they find on Caesar's statues, in an attempt to curb the growing public adoration of Caesar.
keyPoints: 'Images' = statues of Caesar; 'ceremonies' = festive decorations placed on them by the commoners
Flavius and Marullus split up, each taking a different route towards the Capitol
Both tribunes are to strip the decorations off the statues to check Caesar's rising popularity

text: Read the extract: 'Why, man, he doth bestride the narrow world Like a Colossus; and we petty men Walk under his huge legs, and peep about To find ourselves dishonourable graves.' What is referred to as 'a Colossus', and why does Cassius compare Caesar to it?
modelAnswer: The 'Colossus' was a legendary giant bronze statue of the sun-god at Rhodes, so enormous that ships were said to pass between its legs. Cassius compares Caesar to this Colossus to express how Caesar has come to tower over Rome and all other Romans, who now feel like insignificant, 'petty men' scurrying about beneath him, searching only for humble, dishonourable graves rather than any glory of their own. Cassius uses this image to provoke Brutus into feeling that Caesar's dominance has reduced free Romans to nobodies.
keyPoints: The Colossus was a giant statue at Rhodes, large enough for ships to pass beneath
Cassius compares Caesar to the Colossus to show how he now towers over all of Rome
Other Romans are reduced to 'petty men' seeking only humble graves, not glory

text: Read the extract: 'Here will I stand till Caesar pass along, And as a suitor will I give him this. My heart laments that virtue cannot live Out of the teeth of emulation.' Who is Artemidorus, what does he wish to give Caesar, and why?
modelAnswer: Artemidorus is a teacher of rhetoric in Rome who, unlike the conspirators, is loyal to Caesar and has discovered the conspiracy against his life. He plans to hand Caesar a written note (a 'schedule') listing the names of the conspirators, hoping to warn him in time to save his life. He laments that virtue (meaning Caesar) cannot escape the jealous rivalry ('teeth of emulation') of lesser men, and hopes that if Caesar reads his warning, he may yet live; if not, Artemidorus fears that fate has already sided with the traitors.
keyPoints: Artemidorus is a loyal citizen/rhetoric teacher who has learnt of the conspiracy
He waits on the street to hand Caesar a written note naming the conspirators
He hopes his warning will save Caesar's life, fearing fate favours the traitors otherwise

text: Read the extract: 'I would have had thee there and here again Ere I can tell thee what thou shouldst do there. [Aside] O constancy, be strong upon my side...' Where does this scene take place, to whom is Portia speaking, and what does the extract reveal about her state of mind?
modelAnswer: This scene takes place at Brutus's house in Rome. Portia is speaking to Lucius, Brutus's young servant, whom she is trying to send on an errand to the Senate House to find out what is happening, since she senses that Brutus is anxious about something but has not told her the reason. The extract reveals that Portia is extremely agitated and torn with worry — she cannot even clearly tell Lucius what task she wants him to do, and in her aside, she prays for 'constancy' (the strength to keep a secret), admitting that although she has 'a man's mind', she only has 'a woman's might' to control her anxiety.
keyPoints: Portia, at Brutus's house, tries to send Lucius to the Senate House to learn what is happening
She is too agitated to clearly explain the errand, showing her inner turmoil
Her aside reveals she fears giving away the secret of the conspiracy despite her resolve

text: Read the extract: 'O ye gods, Render me worthy of this noble wife! Hark, hark, one knocks. Portia, go in a while And by and by thy bosom shall partake The secrets of my heart.' Who visits Brutus immediately after Portia leaves, and what is the purpose of his visit?
modelAnswer: Immediately after Portia leaves, Brutus's servant Lucius brings in Caius Ligarius, who has come to see Brutus despite being unwell. Caius Ligarius has heard a rumour that Brutus is planning some noble enterprise and, though sick, declares that he would 'follow' Brutus in any venture he undertakes for Rome's honour, even throwing off his sickness at the thought of it. Brutus then reveals, in general terms, that he has an undertaking in mind — effectively recruiting Ligarius, who bears his own personal grudge against Caesar, into the conspiracy.
keyPoints: Caius Ligarius, though unwell, comes to see Brutus after hearing rumours of a noble plan
He declares he will follow Brutus in any venture, even in his sick state
Brutus uses this loyalty to draw Ligarius into the conspiracy against Caesar

text: Read the extract: '...As if they came from several citizens, Writings, all tending to the great opinion That Rome holds of his name, wherein obscurely Caesar's ambition shall be glanced at.' What does 'they' refer to, whom does Cassius assign to deliver the 'Writings', and where does he want them placed?
modelAnswer: 'They' refers to anonymous letters that Cassius plans to forge, written as though they come from ordinary Roman citizens, praising Brutus's reputation while subtly hinting at Caesar's dangerous ambition. Cassius assigns the task of planting these letters to Cinna. He wants one thrown in at Brutus's window, one placed on the statue of old Brutus (Lucius Junius Brutus, founder of the Republic, whose family name carries weight), and one addressed directly to Brutus, all meant to flatter and provoke Brutus into joining the conspiracy against Caesar.
keyPoints: 'They' are forged letters made to look like they come from ordinary citizens
Cassius gives Cinna the task of planting the letters
They are to be placed at Brutus's window, on old Brutus's statue, and addressed to him directly

text: Read the extract: 'Cowards die many times before their deaths; The valiant never taste of death but once. Of all the wonders that I yet have heard. It seems to me most strange that men should fear...' In this scene, how does Calpurnia try to persuade Caesar not to go to the Senate, and what tactic does she use?
modelAnswer: Calpurnia, deeply shaken by ominous happenings in Rome (unnatural births, lionesses whelping in the streets, fierce fiery warriors fighting in the clouds, and her own nightmare of Caesar's statue running with blood) and by the augurers' failure to find a heart in the sacrificed beast, begs Caesar not to leave the house that day. Rather than claiming the danger is real, she cleverly asks him to blame her own 'fear' for keeping him home, taking responsibility onto herself so that Caesar's pride is not wounded by appearing afraid; she even offers to send Mark Antony to the Senate in his place.
keyPoints: Calpurnia lists several unnatural omens witnessed in Rome, including her own nightmare
The augurers find no heart in the sacrificed animal, a bad omen
She tactfully asks Caesar to stay home 'for her fear', not his own, to protect his pride

text: Read the extract: "Wherefore rejoice? What conquest brings he home? What tributaries follow him to Rome, To grace in captive bonds his chariot wheels? You blocks, you stones, you worse than senseless things!" Who is Marullus addressing, and what conquest is referred to in the extract? Why has the conqueror (Caesar) not brought any captives or spoils to Rome by this victory?
modelAnswer: Marullus is addressing the common citizens of Rome who have gathered to celebrate Caesar's return, calling them 'blocks' and 'stones' for their thoughtless joy. The 'conquest' he refers to is Caesar's victory over the sons of Pompey the Great — not over a foreign enemy, but in a civil war against fellow Romans. Because this was a victory in a Roman civil war rather than a conquest of a foreign nation, Caesar brings home no foreign captives or tributary wealth; instead, Marullus reminds the crowd that Pompey's sons were themselves Roman, so there is nothing noble to celebrate, and the crowd's fickleness in cheering Pompey's conqueror after once worshipping Pompey himself is shameful.
keyPoints: Marullus angrily calls the commoners 'blocks' and 'stones' for celebrating thoughtlessly
The 'conquest' is Caesar's civil-war victory over Pompey's sons, not a foreign enemy
No foreign captives or tribute are brought because it was a victory over fellow Romans

text: Read the extract: 'Either there is a civil strife in heaven, Or else the world, too saucy with the gods, Incenses them to send destruction.' Why does Casca say there is 'a civil strife in heaven', and what two of the most horrible sights has he witnessed that night?
modelAnswer: Casca believes the terrible, unnatural storm he has witnessed must mean that the gods themselves are either quarrelling among themselves in heaven, or are angry at mankind's insolence and are sending destruction as punishment. Among the horrible sights he describes are a common slave whose left hand blazed with flame yet did not burn, and a lion that he met near the Capitol, which glared at him and went on its way without attacking — both deeply unnatural occurrences that fill Casca with superstitious dread.
keyPoints: Casca believes the storm shows either strife among the gods, or their anger at human arrogance
He describes a slave's hand blazing with flame yet remaining unburnt
He also describes meeting a lion near the Capitol that strangely ignored him

text: Read the extract: 'Alas! my Lord. Your wisdom is consum'd in confidence. Do not go forth today: call it my fear That keeps you in the house, and not your own.' State two unusual things Calpurnia had heard of that made her fearful, and explain how Decius Brutus later interprets her nightmare to persuade Caesar to go to the Senate anyway.
modelAnswer: Calpurnia has heard that a lioness has whelped (given birth) in the open streets, that graves have opened up and yielded their dead, and that fierce warriors fought in fiery formations in the clouds above the Capitol — all terrifying omens. She has also dreamt that Caesar's statue, like a fountain with a hundred spouts, ran pure blood, in which smiling Romans bathed their hands. When Caesar nearly decides to stay home because of this, Decius Brutus cleverly reinterprets the dream as a favourable one: he says it signifies that Rome will draw renewed life and strength from Caesar, and that Romans will eagerly seek relics and signs of favour from him — flattering Caesar's vanity and persuading him to go to the Senate after all.
keyPoints: Calpurnia's fears: a lioness whelping in the streets, graves yielding the dead, warriors fighting in the clouds
Her nightmare: Caesar's statue spouting blood in which Romans bathed their hands
Decius flatters Caesar by reinterpreting the dream as Rome drawing life/strength from him, luring him to the Senate

text: Read the extract: 'Their logs held tight in death's still hands Was proof of human sin. They did not die from the cold without They died from the cold within.' Who are 'they', and what is the message the poet wants to convey through the poem?
modelAnswer: 'They' are the six strangers who sat huddled in a circle around a dying campfire during a bitter winter night, each holding a log of wood that could have kept the fire burning. Each person refused to share their log out of a different prejudice — racial, religious, class, selfishness, laziness, and vengefulness — and as a result, they all froze to death clutching their logs, even though together their wood could easily have kept the fire alive. The poet's message is that human prejudice, selfishness and indifference towards others — the 'cold within' the human heart — is far more deadly and destructive than any physical cold or hardship from outside.
keyPoints: 'They' are six strangers who each withheld their log from the dying fire out of a different prejudice
Each person's selfishness or bias caused them all to freeze to death together
The poem's message: human coldness of heart (prejudice, selfishness) is more deadly than physical cold

text: Read the extract: 'For oft, when on my couch I lie In vacant or in pensive mood They flash upon that inward eye Which is the bliss of solitude; And then my heart with pleasure fills, And dances with the daffodils.' What 'wealth' does the poet refer to in the poem, and how was this wealth brought to him?
modelAnswer: The 'wealth' the poet (Wordsworth) refers to is the lasting joy and inner richness that the memory of the golden daffodils he once saw dancing beside a lake has given him. He did not realise, at the time he saw the dancing flowers, what emotional wealth the sight would bring him. This wealth is brought to him later, whenever he lies at rest in a thoughtful or idle mood: the memory of the daffodils flashes upon his 'inward eye' (his imagination/memory), filling his heart with pleasure, so that in spirit he 'dances with the daffodils' all over again, long after the actual sight has passed.
keyPoints: The 'wealth' is the lasting joy that the memory of the daffodils gives the poet
He did not recognise this wealth at the moment of seeing them
The memory later returns to him in solitude, filling his heart with renewed pleasure

text: Read the extract: 'With fire and sword the country round Was wasted far and wide, And many a childing mother then, And new-born baby died; But things like that, you know, must be At every famous victory.' Who is the speaker, how was the country affected by the war, and how does the young generation (Peterkin and Wilhelmine) respond to the horrors described?
modelAnswer: The speaker is old Kaspar, recalling the Battle of Blenheim to his grandchildren, Peterkin and Wilhelmine. He describes how the countryside was devastated by fire and sword, homes were burnt, and many pregnant mothers and new-born babies died in the chaos of war — yet he dismisses this suffering with the resigned phrase that 'things like that must be' at every famous victory. The children, however, are untouched by the horror of what he describes; Wilhelmine simply says 'it was a wicked thing', while Peterkin innocently and eagerly asks what good came out of the famous victory, showing that the young generation cannot grasp the true cost of war and are more curious about the 'glory' of it than horrified by its destruction.
keyPoints: Kaspar describes widespread destruction, and the deaths of mothers and infants, from the war
He excuses this suffering as something that 'must be' at every famous victory
The children fail to grasp the horror, with Peterkin instead asking what good came of the victory

text: Read the extract: 'Bangle sellers are we who bear Our shining loads to the temple fair... Who will buy these delicate, bright Rainbow-tinted circles of light? Lustrous tokens of radiant lives, For happy daughters and happy wives.' Explain, in your own words, the phrases 'shining loads' and 'lustrous tokens of radiant lives', and explain what colours the poet associates with a maiden and with a middle-aged woman respectively.
modelAnswer: 'Shining loads' refers to the baskets of brightly coloured, glittering bangles that the sellers carry to sell at the temple fair. 'Lustrous tokens of radiant lives' means that the bangles are seen as bright, shining symbols or markers of the different joyful stages of a woman's life, since Indian women traditionally wear bangles to mark happy occasions. The poet associates the maiden (young unmarried girl) with bangles of silver and blue, reflecting her innocent dreams and the carefree rapture of her tender youth, while she associates the middle-aged woman (who has borne children) with bangles of purple and gold, reflecting her mature pride as a mother who has given her husband sons and shares in his triumphs.
keyPoints: 'Shining loads' = baskets of bright, colourful bangles the sellers carry
'Lustrous tokens of radiant lives' = bangles symbolising the happy stages of a woman's life
The poet links silver-blue bangles with a maiden's dreams, and purple-gold with a mother's mature pride

chapter: Literature — The Heart of the Tree
text: Read the extract: 'He plants a friend of sun and sky; He plants the flag of breezes free;' Explain how a tree is a 'friend of sun and sky', and how he who plants a tree 'plants the flag of breezes free'.
modelAnswer: A tree is called 'a friend of sun and sky' because it grows upward towards the sun and sky, offering them its leaves and branches, and in turn receives sunlight and open air to flourish — it exists in harmony with these natural elements, giving shade from the sun and reaching towards the open sky. The tree 'plants the flag of breezes free' because its tall branches and leaves sway and rustle freely in the wind, like a flag fluttering in the breeze, standing as a visible symbol of nature's freedom and of the person's loyalty to the land and to future generations who will enjoy its shade and beauty.
keyPoints: The tree reaches towards the sun and open sky, living in harmony with them and offering shade
Its swaying branches/leaves in the wind are compared to a flag fluttering freely
This 'flag' symbolises freedom, civic loyalty, and a gift to future generations

text: Read the extract: ''All right!' you'll cry. 'All right!' you'll say, 'But if we take the set away, What shall we do to entertain Our darling children? Please explain!'' (Roald Dahl, 'Television'). What important lesson does the poet say he has learnt, and what other activity does he recommend to entertain children instead of watching television?
modelAnswer: The poet begins by saying he has learnt, above everything else, that children should never, ever be allowed to watch television — or at least their watching should be severely limited — because it rots their brains and turns their minds to mush, dulling their imagination and senses. As an alternative, he strongly recommends that parents fill their house with books instead, so that children develop the habit of reading. He argues that if a bookshelf full of books is simply made available, children will eventually feel curious enough to pick one up and start reading, and will then discover far richer worlds of imagination than television could ever offer.
keyPoints: The poet's chief lesson: children should not be allowed to watch television, as it harms their minds
He recommends filling the house with books as the healthier alternative
He believes that simply having books around will eventually draw curious children to read

text: Read the extract: 'I remember, I remember, Where I was used to swing, And thought the air must rush as fresh To swallows on the wing; My spirit flew in feathers then, That is so heavy now, And summer pools could hardly cool The fever on my brow!' What is 'that' which 'is so heavy now', and what contrast does the poet draw between his childhood and his present state?
modelAnswer: 'That' refers to the poet's spirit, which he says 'flew in feathers' — felt light, free and joyous — when he was a child swinging and imagining himself as free as a swallow in flight. In contrast, in his present adult life, that same spirit has become 'heavy', weighed down by the cares, worries and disappointments of growing up. The poet draws a clear contrast between the carefree lightness and boundless joy of childhood, when even the heat of summer could be cooled by simple pleasures, and his present burdened, joyless adult state, where such simple pleasures no longer have the power to lift his spirit.
keyPoints: 'That' = the poet's spirit, once light and free like a bird, now heavy with adult cares
As a child, his spirit was joyous and carefree while swinging
The contrast highlights how adulthood has weighed down the lightness and joy he once felt

text: Read the extract: 'I remember, I remember, The fir trees dark and high. I used to think their slender tops Were close against the sky: It was a childish ignorance, But now 'tis little joy To know I'm farther off from heaven Than when I was a boy.' What was the poet's childhood view of the fir trees, and what does he mean by 'childish ignorance'? Why is the final line significant?
modelAnswer: As a child, the poet believed that the tall, slender tops of the fir trees near his home actually touched the sky, standing close against heaven itself. He calls this innocent, mistaken belief 'childish ignorance' — the naive, literal way children see and understand the world around them, without the burden of adult knowledge or disillusionment. The final line, 'Than when I was a boy', is significant because it is deeply ironic: though the poet has grown physically taller and gained more worldly knowledge as an adult, he feels he has moved spiritually and emotionally 'farther off from heaven' — that is, he has lost the innocence, purity and closeness to goodness that he had as an unspoiled child, so growing up has brought him no real joy.
keyPoints: As a child, the poet believed the fir trees' tops touched the sky
'Childish ignorance' = the innocent, mistaken but pure way children perceive the world
The final line is ironic: growing older has taken him 'farther', not closer, to heavenly innocence

text: Read the extract: 'But Skimble's just behind him and was ready to remind him, For Skimble won't let anything go wrong. And when you creep into your cosy berth And pull up the counterpane You ought to reflect that it's very nice To know that you won't be bothered by mice— You can leave all that to the Railway Cat, The Cat of the Railway Train!' Mention any three comforts on the train that are ensured by Skimbleshanks, and explain how he ensures the train runs smoothly.
modelAnswer: Skimbleshanks ensures several comforts for passengers travelling on the Night Mail: he makes sure mice will not trouble them in their berths, he checks that each sleeping compartment is properly equipped (soap, towels, a labelled corner for their name), and he supervises that the tea-making equipment is all in working order for the morning. He ensures the train runs smoothly by constantly patrolling up and down its corridors throughout the night, personally examining the faces of the passengers, checking on the staff and guards, and keeping a watchful, almost supervisory eye on every detail of the journey so that nothing ever goes wrong while he is 'in charge'.
keyPoints: Comforts: freedom from mice, properly stocked berths, and ready tea-making arrangements
Skimble constantly patrols the length of the train through the night
He personally checks on passengers and staff, taking responsibility like someone truly in charge

text: Read the extract: 'The gradient's against her, but she's on time. Past cotton-grass and moorland boulder Shovelling white steam over her shoulder, Snorting noisily as she passes Silent miles of wind-bent grasses.' What is meant by the term 'gradient', why is it 'against her', and what is the significance of the word 'but' in the first line?
modelAnswer: The 'gradient' refers to the upward slope of the track the train has to climb, which makes the engine's job harder as it works against gravity. It is 'against her' because climbing uphill requires more effort and slows a train down, working against its timely progress. The word 'but' is significant because it shows that despite this difficulty — the uphill climb working against it — the train (personified as 'she') still manages to stay exactly on time, highlighting the reliability, power and determination of the night mail train even under difficult conditions.
keyPoints: 'Gradient' = the uphill slope of the railway track, which slows the train down
It works 'against' the train by making the climb harder
'But' emphasises that despite this difficulty, the train still arrives exactly on time

chapter: Literature — A Horse and Two Goats
text: Read the extract: 'You have only four teeth in your jaw, but your craving is for big things. All right, get the stuff for the sauce, and I will prepare it for you.' What was Muni craving for, and under what condition does his wife agree to prepare it for him?
modelAnswer: Muni, in R.K. Narayan's story 'A Horse and Two Goats', is craving a drumstick vegetable sauce, even though he has only four teeth left in his old age and little ability to chew hard food. His wife teases him about this mismatch between his few teeth and his craving for such an elaborate dish, but agrees to prepare the sauce for him only on the condition that he first goes out and brings back the ingredients — specifically, he must obtain the necessary items (such as drumsticks, chilli, dhal and other items) from the shop himself, since she has none in the house and no money to buy them.
keyPoints: Muni craves a drumstick sauce despite having only four teeth
His wife mocks the gap between his poor teeth and his elaborate craving
She agrees to cook it only if he first fetches the ingredients from the shop himself

chapter: Literature — A Horse and Two Goats
text: Read the extract: 'Muni sat at the foot of the statue, watching his two goats graze in the arid soil among the cactus and lantana bushes.' Where is Muni, what advantage did his presence there give him, and what difference in financial status exists between Muni and the foreigner he later meets?
modelAnswer: Muni is sitting at the foot of a large clay statue of a horse, on the outskirts of his tiny, poverty-stricken village, grazing his two goats on the dry, barren land nearby. Sitting beside the statue gives him some shelter and shade, and a reasonably central vantage point from where he can watch over his goats while they graze among the sparse vegetation. Muni is extremely poor — he and his wife survive on meagre means, often going without a proper meal, and the goats are practically his only possessions — whereas the American foreigner who later arrives is clearly wealthy, well-dressed and equipped with a car and camera, so their chance meeting at the statue highlights the vast gulf between poverty and material prosperity, and between Eastern and Western cultures.
keyPoints: Muni sits at the foot of a clay horse statue outside his village, grazing his two goats
The spot offers him shade and a vantage point to watch his goats
Muni is desperately poor, in sharp contrast to the wealthy, car-owning American foreigner

text: Read the extract: ''It's a cruel thing to leave her so.' 'Then take her to the poorhouse: she'll have to go there,' answered the blacksmith's wife, springing away, and leaving Joe behind.' Who are having this conversation, and what kind of man was Joe Thompson, based on his reaction to Maggie's situation?
modelAnswer: This conversation is between Joe Thompson and the blacksmith's wife, discussing what should be done with Maggie, the crippled, orphaned child left behind after her mother's death from neglect and vice. The blacksmith's wife callously suggests sending Maggie to the poorhouse and walks away, unwilling to take responsibility. Joe Thompson, however, is shown to be a basically kind-hearted though rough and gruff man — he hesitates, feeling it would be 'cruel' to abandon the helpless child, and eventually his conscience moves him to take Maggie into his own home with his wife, revealing a softness and sense of compassion beneath his rough exterior.
keyPoints: The blacksmith's wife and Joe Thompson discuss what to do with the orphaned, crippled Maggie
The wife callously suggests the poorhouse and walks away
Joe, though rough-mannered, shows compassion by hesitating to abandon the helpless child

chapter: Literature — The Old Man at the Bridge
text: Read the extract: 'There were three animals altogether,' he explained. 'There were two goats and a cat and then there were four pairs of pigeons.' Who is 'he', why is he sitting by the roadside unable to walk further, and what advice does the narrator give him?
modelAnswer: 'He' is an old man, a refugee fleeing the fighting near the Ebro River during the Spanish Civil War, who has been forced to abandon his home and his small animals — two goats, a cat, and four pairs of pigeons — which he was caring for. He is sitting exhausted by the side of the road, too tired and too worried about his abandoned animals to walk any further towards safety, even as enemy forces draw closer. The narrator, who is scouting the bridge for the advancing army, advises the old man to get up and walk on to escape the approaching danger, but the old man, overwhelmed by exhaustion and grief for his animals, says he cannot, highlighting how war disrupts and destroys the simple lives of ordinary people.
keyPoints: The old man is a refugee who has had to abandon his two goats, a cat and pigeons
He is too exhausted and worried about his animals to walk further
The narrator urges him to move on to safety, but the old man feels he cannot

chapter: Literature — A Face in the Dark
text: Read the extract: 'What are you doing out here, boy?' asked Mr. Oliver sharply, moving closer so that he could recognize the miscreant. But even as he approached the boy, Mr. Oliver senses that something was wrong. Who was Mr. Oliver, where did he work, and how does Ruskin Bond use supernatural elements to create mystery and horror in the story?
modelAnswer: Mr. Oliver was an Anglo-Indian schoolteacher at a boys' school in the hills, nicknamed the 'Eton of the East' for its reputation and prestige. Walking back to school at night through a lonely pine forest, he comes upon what seems to be a schoolboy crying silently by the path. When he gets close enough to see the boy's face properly, he is horrified to find that the boy has no eyes, nose or mouth — just a smooth, blank oval where his face should be. Ruskin Bond builds mystery and horror gradually: first through the boy's unnaturally soundless crying, then the terrifying absence of a face, and finally through the watchman who, when Mr. Oliver flees to him for help, turns and reveals that same blank face, suggesting the horror cannot be escaped and may not have been merely a trick of the imagination.
keyPoints: Mr. Oliver is a schoolteacher at a prestigious hill school, the 'Eton of the East'
He encounters a crying boy in the forest who, on closer look, has no face at all
The watchman he flees to also reveals a blank face, deepening the horror and suggesting it was not imagined

text: Read the extract: 'The girl's eyes, fascinated, went back, widening a little, to rest upon the glittering handcuffs. 'Don't you worry about them, miss,' said the other man.' Who were handcuffed and why, and in what way does the story justify the saying 'appearances can be deceptive'?
modelAnswer: In O. Henry's story, two men, Mr. Easton and a rough-looking man named Mr. Bob, are handcuffed together, with Mr. Easton appearing to be the elegant gentleman and the other man seemingly his captive outlaw prisoner, being taken to Leavenworth prison by a marshal. In fact, the story cleverly reverses expectations: it is Mr. Easton, the polished and well-dressed man whom Miss Fairchild assumes is a respectable marshal escorting a criminal, who is actually the prisoner being taken to jail for forgery; the rough-looking 'glum-faced man' is, in reality, the marshal. This twist perfectly illustrates that appearances can be deceptive, since outward elegance or roughness says nothing reliable about a person's true character or situation.
keyPoints: Easton and the rough-looking man are handcuffed together on the train
Miss Fairchild assumes the well-dressed Easton is the marshal and the rough man his prisoner
The twist reveals Easton is actually the prisoner, and the rough man the marshal — appearances deceive

text: Read the extract: 'The master hit Oliver with his spoon, then seized him and cried for help. Mr Bumble rushed into the room, and the master told him what Oliver had said.' What unusual thing did Oliver do, what was the master's reaction, and what does the notice later put up on the workhouse gate reveal about life in that era?
modelAnswer: The 'unusual' thing Oliver did was to dare to ask the master for more gruel after finishing his meagre portion, driven by the desperate, constant hunger suffered by the workhouse boys. The master reacts with shock and outrage at Oliver's audacity, striking him with the serving spoon and shouting for help, as if Oliver had committed a grave crime simply by being hungry and asking for food. Afterwards, a notice is put up on the workhouse gate offering a reward of five pounds to anyone who would take Oliver off the parish's hands — revealing how little orphaned, poor children were valued in nineteenth-century England, and how institutions like the workhouse treated basic hunger as a punishable offence rather than a need to be met.
keyPoints: Oliver dares to ask for more gruel after his meagre portion, driven by extreme hunger
The master reacts with shock and violence, treating the request as a serious offence
The reward notice on the gate shows how little value was placed on poor orphaned children

text: Read the extract: 'When Hughie came in, he found Trevor putting the finishing touches to a wonderful life-size picture of a beggar-man. The beggar himself was standing on a raised platform in a corner of the studio.' Who was Trevor, describe the beggar modelling for him, and what vital information does Hughie later learn about the beggar?
modelAnswer: Alan Trevor is a talented painter and a close friend of Hughie Erskine. The beggar modelling for him is described as an old man in ragged, miserable clothes, with a wrinkled, pathetic, sorrowful face — the very picture of poverty and misfortune, which makes Hughie feel immediate pity for him. Later, when Hughie meets Trevor again at his club that evening, he learns the astonishing truth that the beggar is not poor at all — he is, in reality, a Baron and an immensely wealthy millionaire who simply enjoys posing as a beggar for painters as an unusual hobby, which makes Hughie's earlier act of generosity towards him all the more ironic and ultimately rewarding.
keyPoints: Alan Trevor is a talented painter and Hughie's good friend
The beggar-model appears pitiably poor, in rags, with a sorrowful face
Hughie later learns the 'beggar' is actually a wealthy millionaire posing for fun

text: Read the extract: 'Well I think the model should have a percentage,' cried Hughie, laughing... Who is the protagonist of 'The Model Millionaire', and why does Hughie give the old beggar-model a sovereign despite having very little money himself?
modelAnswer: The protagonist of Oscar Wilde's story is Hughie Erskine, a charming, good-natured young man who has every accomplishment except the ability to make money, and who is desperately in love with Laura Merton but cannot marry her as he lacks the ten thousand pounds her father demands as a condition. Despite having almost no money of his own, Hughie is deeply moved by what he believes is the old model's genuine poverty and sorrowful appearance, and in a moment of pure generosity and compassion, he gives the 'beggar' his only sovereign (gold coin) — an act which, ironically, later earns him great reward when the 'beggar' turns out to be a wealthy Baron who repays Hughie's kindness many times over.
keyPoints: Hughie Erskine is the warm-hearted but perpetually penniless protagonist
He is in love with Laura but cannot afford to marry her
Moved by pity for the apparently poor model, he generously gives him his only sovereign

text: Read the extract: 'Bonku Babu did not know what to say. He was feeling quite uncomfortable, for the creature had reached out and was examining Bonku Babu's arms and legs with its long, bony fingers.' Who was the creature Bonku Babu meets, and how does this encounter change him by the end of the story?
modelAnswer: The creature Bonku Babu meets is Ang, an alien visitor from the planet Craneus whose spaceship has landed secretly in a bamboo grove near Bonku Babu's village. Ang is highly intelligent, knows thousands of languages, and shows Bonku Babu extraordinary sights from around the world through a special viewing device, as well as demonstrating his superior physical and mental abilities compared to humans. Bonku Babu, who was previously a timid, mild-mannered schoolteacher often mocked and looked down upon by his fellow villagers for his meekness, is transformed by this secret encounter: inspired by Ang's wisdom and his own renewed sense of self-worth after being chosen for this extraordinary meeting, he grows noticeably more confident and self-assured in his daily dealings with others.
keyPoints: Ang is an alien from the planet Craneus whose spaceship secretly lands near the village
Ang shows Bonku Babu wonders from around the world and displays superior abilities
The once-timid Bonku Babu gains confidence and self-assurance after this life-changing encounter

chapter: Literature — The Boy who Broke the Bank
text: Read the extract: ''I don't wish to talk about it,' complained the sweeper-boy. 'I haven't even received my regular pay. And this is the twentieth of the month. Who would think a bank would hold up a poor man's salary?'' What does Nathu not want to talk about, and how does the eventual rumour and panic about the bank turn out to be ironic?
modelAnswer: Nathu, the young sweeper-boy at the bank, does not wish to talk about his continuing frustration over his unpaid salary, which is already overdue by the twentieth of the month, showing his growing resentment at the bank's apparent carelessness towards its own humble employee. The story's irony lies in the fact that Nathu's harmless, offhand complaints about the bank's financial troubles are overheard and misunderstood by passers-by, who begin spreading a rumour that the bank is going bankrupt; this baseless rumour then causes a genuine panic, with crowds rushing to withdraw their money, nearly causing the very bank failure that was never actually true in the first place — an ordinary boy's grumbling accidentally almost 'breaks the bank'.
keyPoints: Nathu complains about his own salary being overdue, unrelated to the bank's real finances
His careless remarks are overheard and twisted into a rumour that the bank is failing
The irony: a baseless rumour from an innocent complaint nearly causes the very collapse it falsely predicted

text: Read the extract: 'The next morning Phatik was nowhere to be seen. All searches in the neighbourhood proved futile. The rain had been pouring in torrents all night, and those who went out in search of the boy got drenched through to the skin.' Why was Phatik 'nowhere to be seen', what compelled him to take this decision, and how was his life in Calcutta different from that in his village?
modelAnswer: Phatik had secretly run away from his uncle's house in Calcutta, desperate to escape back to his home village, because he could no longer bear the constant ill-treatment, scolding and unkindness he suffered at the hands of his aunt, who resented having to look after him and treated him with open hostility, making him feel like an unwanted burden in the household. In his village, Phatik had once been free, boisterous and the carefree ringleader of his group of friends, enjoying open fields and the freedom to play; in Calcutta, however, he is confined, friendless, constantly humiliated, and treated as an inferior guest in his own relative's home, with none of the freedom or belonging he once knew, which eventually drives him to flee in the pouring rain.
keyPoints: Phatik secretly runs away, desperate to return home after his aunt's constant ill-treatment
He is searched for unsuccessfully through a night of heavy rain
Unlike his free, happy village life, his life in Calcutta is lonely, confined and humiliating

text: Read the extract: 'Bonku Babu broke out into goose pimples, but an irrepressible curiosity drove him further forward. As he went past a cluster of bamboo stems, an object came into view.' Describe what Bonku Babu saw as the object came into view, and in what ways did the creature he met prove to be superior to humans.
modelAnswer: As Bonku Babu moved cautiously forward past the bamboo stems, he saw a strange, giant, glowing glass object resting in the middle of the bamboo grove, emitting an eerie pink light — which turns out to be an alien spaceship. The creature he meets, Ang, proves superior to humans in several striking ways: he can effortlessly master thousands of languages (unlike humans who struggle to learn even a few), he possesses a special tube-like device that lets him instantly show faraway places and sights from across the world, and he demonstrates calm, controlled, and highly advanced intelligence far beyond ordinary human capability, all of which leaves Bonku Babu astonished.
keyPoints: Bonku Babu sees a giant, glowing glass object (a spaceship) in the bamboo grove
The alien, Ang, knows thousands of languages effortlessly
Ang can show faraway sights through a special device, displaying vastly superior abilities

text: Read the passage about a youngster who quit Facebook (from a Unit Test comprehension passage). What changes were observed in the life of the youngster after he quit Facebook, and why did he call Facebook 'a recipe for disaster'?
modelAnswer: After quitting Facebook, the youngster felt relieved of the pressure of maintaining an online image, since the new 'timeline' feature would have exposed old, embarrassing posts and comments from his past that he had since outgrown and no longer wanted others to see. He calls Facebook 'a recipe for disaster' because the timeline feature compresses years of someone's history into an easily browsable, chronological record, meaning that friends could instantly revisit old posts, photos or comments that he now found embarrassing, with no way for him to control or hide this exposure of his past self.
keyPoints: He felt relief at escaping constant exposure of his past posts and comments
The 'timeline' feature made years of old posts easily browsable by anyone
He feared friends re-discovering embarrassing posts from his past that no longer reflected him

text: Read the passage about 'Uncle Jules' (from a Unit Test comprehension passage). How did the narrator's parents react after recognising Jules on the ship, and why?
modelAnswer: When the narrator's father realised that the shabby, poverty-stricken old sailor opening oysters on the ship's deck was in fact Uncle Jules — the very relative whose promised wealthy return the family had been hoping for and boasting about for years — he was deeply shocked and murmured 'What a catastrophe!' Both parents became visibly upset and anxious, and they immediately decided that, especially in front of the narrator's brother-in-law, none of them would acknowledge Jules as a family member at all. They reacted this way out of shame and fear of social embarrassment, since admitting that their once-promising rich uncle had actually become a poor, ragged sailor would have humiliated the family in front of relatives and damaged their social standing.
keyPoints: The father is shocked to recognise the shabby sailor as the long-awaited rich Uncle Jules
Both parents become anxious and decide not to acknowledge him as family
Their reaction stems from shame and fear of social embarrassment in front of the brother-in-law

text: Read the passage about the 'Law of the Garbage Truck' (from a Unit Test comprehension passage). How did the taxi driver avert an accident, and to what did he compare the yelling driver?
modelAnswer: The taxi driver averted the accident by slamming on his brakes and skidding just in time, narrowly missing by inches the other car that had suddenly pulled out of a parking space in front of them. He compared the yelling, angry driver to a 'garbage truck' — explaining that many people are like garbage trucks, carrying around a load of anger, frustration and disappointment, which eventually piles up so much that they need to 'dump' it somewhere, sometimes unfairly onto innocent people who happen to be nearby.
keyPoints: The taxi driver slammed on the brakes and skidded, narrowly avoiding a collision
He compares the angry, yelling driver to a 'garbage truck' full of built-up anger
His point: people often unfairly dump their accumulated frustration onto others

text: Read the passage from Jerome K. Jerome's 'Three Men in a Boat' describing the narrator, George and Harris packing for a trip. In not more than 50 words, describe the comical packing experiences of the three men.
modelAnswer: The narrator struggles for ages searching for his lost toothbrush amid the chaos of packing. When George and Harris take over, they immediately break a cup, squash strawberry jam onto a tomato, and George steps on the butter. They then search frantically all over the room for the missing butter, finally discovering it stuck to the chair Harris had unknowingly sat on, before finally managing to pack it away in the teapot.
keyPoints: The narrator wastes time hunting for his lost toothbrush
George and Harris break a cup and squash jam onto a tomato while packing
They lose the butter (stuck under Harris) before finally stuffing it into the teapot

text: In the same 'Three Men in a Boat' passage, what is the narrator's picture of things before the creation of the world, and why was the toothbrush a thing that haunted him?
modelAnswer: The narrator says that after turning out every item from the bags while searching for his toothbrush, the room ended up in much the same jumbled, chaotic state as things must have been in before the world was created — a vivid image of utter disorder and confusion. The toothbrush haunts him because he is constantly plagued by the anxious fear, every time he travels, that he has forgotten to pack it; this fear is so persistent that he dreams about it, and ends up endlessly repacking and unpacking the bag just to be sure of its whereabouts.
keyPoints: He compares the chaotic room to the state of the world before creation
The toothbrush haunts him because he constantly fears having forgotten to pack it
This anxiety makes him dream about it and repeatedly repack his bag

text: Read the passage about Doctor Faustus. In not more than 50 words, describe Faustus' realization of the sin he committed and his appeal for repentance.
modelAnswer: As his twenty-four years of power drew to a close, an old man's rebuke made Faustus feel the full weight of his sin. He realized he had sacrificed eternal joy for fleeting pleasures, and bitterly regretted signing away his soul. With only an hour left, he desperately begged the planets to stop moving and appealed to God for mercy, hoping to repent in time.
keyPoints: An old man's scolding awakens Faustus's sense of sin and guilt
He realizes he traded eternal joy for twenty-four years of empty pleasure
He begs time itself to stop and appeals to God for mercy before his damnation

text: In the Doctor Faustus passage, what was the deal Faustus signed with Lucifer, and what did Faustus do immediately after his offer was accepted?
modelAnswer: Faustus signed a deal, written in his own blood, promising to give his soul to Lucifer in exchange for twenty-four years of unlimited magical power, wealth and pleasures, with the devil Mephistophilis serving him throughout that period. Once the offer was accepted and the deal sealed, Faustus immediately began using his new powers to travel the heavens and earth in a chariot drawn by dragons, performing tricks and illusions that made him a famous and celebrated magician and scholar.
keyPoints: Faustus signed the deal in his own blood, offering his soul for 24 years of power
Mephistophilis would serve him throughout this period
He immediately began travelling and performing magic tricks, gaining fame as a magician

text: Read the passage about Cameron Mounger and the signed dollar note. In not more than 50 words, explain how Cameron's life changed when he made his greatest sacrifice.
modelAnswer: Cameron gave his treasured, star-signed dollar note to a stranded old man in desperate need of money for food. That very morning, opportunities began flowing in unexpectedly: a lucrative advertising offer, followed by more work. Soon his career flourished; he built a successful car repair business, had a baby with his wife, and built a comfortable home — all stemming from that one selfless act of giving.
keyPoints: Cameron gives away his treasured signed dollar note to help a desperate stranger
Immediately afterwards, unexpected opportunities (a paid advertisement) start coming his way
His life steadily improves — career success, marriage, a home — all following this sacrifice

text: In the Cameron Mounger passage, on what did Cameron get autographs from country music stars, and why was he initially reluctant to give the old man a dollar note?
modelAnswer: Cameron collected autographs from country music stars on an ordinary one-dollar note, since he did not have any paper handy for them to sign on the night he was taken backstage after a show in Nashville; he treasured this signed dollar note ever afterwards as a keepsake. He was initially reluctant to give the old stranded man a dollar because it was the same precious, autographed note he had kept for years as a memento, and also because he himself was going through financial hardship at the time, barely having enough money for petrol to get home.
keyPoints: He got the autographs on an ordinary dollar note, having no paper to hand
The note held years of sentimental, treasured value for him
He was also himself struggling financially, with barely enough money for petrol

text: Read the passage about the black heron and the photographer. Mention two possible reasons for the birds' extraordinary wing-covering behaviour, and explain why the writer wanted Peter to film them from the road.
modelAnswer: The writer suggests that the herons were covering themselves with their wings either to create a sudden darkness that would confuse and disorient the small fish they were hunting, or to shade their own eyes from the sun's glare reflecting off the water's surface, helping them see their prey more clearly underwater. The writer wanted Peter to film the birds from the road, using a telephoto lens, because the birds were already accustomed to the ordinary movement of cars and people along the road and would not be alarmed by it, whereas approaching them more closely on foot would likely frighten them away and disrupt their feeding.
keyPoints: Possible reasons: confusing fish with sudden darkness, or shading their eyes from water glare
Birds were used to vehicles and people on the road, so filming from there would not alarm them
Approaching too closely on foot risked scaring the herons away from their feeding

text: Read the passage about young Boris Becker. According to the narrator, what were the most remarkable features of Becker that he can recall from their first meeting, and what, in the narrator's opinion, caused Boris to fail his trial?
modelAnswer: The narrator recalls that what was truly remarkable about the young Boris Becker was not his physical skill — he was overweight, clumsy and used no proper footwork — but the extraordinary intensity of his eyes and his concentration: he stared at every oncoming ball with a fierce, almost impossible focus that most children, easily distracted by anything around them, simply did not have. The narrator believes Boris failed the formal trial because the official trainers' checklist only measured things like running speed and technique, with nothing on it to measure 'eyes' or powers of concentration — the very qualities that actually made Boris exceptional but that the standard test could not detect.
keyPoints: Boris's eyes and extraordinary concentration while playing, despite clumsy technique, stood out most
The official trial only tested physical measures like running and technique
Because concentration/focus wasn't on the checklist, his true talent went unnoticed and he failed

text: Read the extract from 'Village by the Sea' by Anita Desai. Who were the Vakils, and why was the house (Mon Repos) more suited to the de Silva family than to the Vakils?
modelAnswer: The Vakils were a Bombay family who had been among the first to build holiday cottages on the Thul beach, and who originally owned the house called Mon Repos before selling it to the de Silvas a year before the story's events. The house became more suited to the de Silvas because, unlike the Vakils, who had 'grown too old and frail' to travel and enjoy the beach house often, the de Silvas were young, energetic people who genuinely loved spending their holidays there, bringing the house to lively use rather than leaving it standing empty for most of the year as the ageing Vakils had done.
keyPoints: The Vakils were an old Bombay family who originally built and owned Mon Repos
They had grown too old and frail to visit the house often, so it stood empty
The young, energetic de Silvas actually enjoy and use the beach house, unlike the ageing Vakils
